We introduce PeptSol, an open benchmark of 1388 hand-curated protected-peptide solubility measurements with chemistry-aware splits. The measurements span only 84 parent sequences and 101 protected structures, and 92.5% come from a single historical programme. Across seven frozen molecular encoders, the best macro-F1 is 0.843 on binary solubility for the historical subset under a peptide-held-out split; the harder three-class ordinal task reaches 0.614 in that cell. No foundation model consistently outperforms a baseline combining chemical fingerprints with explicit molecular descriptors, and model rankings vary across prediction tasks and data splits. The dataset, evaluation protocol, and baselines establish a standard for measuring progress on molecular representations for synthesis-aware peptide developability.
Biomolecules.comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 19 tables. Accepted at the AI for Drug Discovery workshop, NeurIPS 2026

QM.title: Agentic Literature Extraction Augments Targeted Protein Degradation Databases
QM.summary: Predictive models in medicinal chemistry depend on structured assay data locked in primary publications. This bottleneck is acute in targeted protein degradation (TPD), where each assay record must combine compound identity, degradation target, recruiter, assay context, and endpoint values reported across sections, tables, and supplementary files. Existing TPD databases are manually curated and often lack assay context. We present an expert-in-the-loop large language model workflow in which a cross-validated prompt-refinement module adapts extraction instructions from scarce expert annotations. With only seven annotated molecular glue publications, the workflow achieved record-level $F_1 = 0.98$ and transferred to proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) by terminology substitution alone ($F_1 \geq 0.93$). The resulting database, AutoTPD, contained 81% and 92% more molecular glue and PROTAC records than standardized reference datasets; expert audits found 92/100 and 33/40 new records to be correct. Applying the workflow to eligible PubMed Central open-access literature added 4,483 records from 598 publications, yielding AutoTPD+, a public, versioned database of 7,622 TPD records, including degradation assay measurements, designed for monthly updates. In a controlled surrogate model comparison, PROTAC degradation activity models trained on AutoTPD+ saw a 8.9-18.2% error reduction relative to models trained on the original PROTAC-DB data.

QM.title: A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation
QM.summary: Real-time phase estimation on stimulus-aligned transient EEG is critical for closed-loop neuromodulation systems targeting the theta-band, yet most real-time phase estimation methods have been developed and validated on resting-state, high-fidelity signals in the alpha band. Recent work has pursued deep learning architectures, while individualized classical bandpass filter tuning remains underexplored. This study characterizes the spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering and demonstrates the performance gains achieved through individualized tuning. We present a Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model evaluated on EEG recorded during peripheral vibrotactile stimulation of the left median nerve (theta, N=20 healthy subjects) and on resting-state recordings from the Max Planck Institute's LEMON dataset (alpha, N=20 healthy subjects). BOB was benchmarked against the Deep Dual-Branch Complex Neural Network (DBCNN), EEG Phase Prediction Network (EPN), Phastimate, and Phase Estimation with Autoregressive Padding (PEAP) under matched testing conditions: channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation time points, and an offline reference phase obtained through zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform. Under these testing conditions, BOB achieved matched or better performance than these models at a fraction of the calibration time.
QM.comment: 24 pages, 12 figures (9 main, 3 supplements)

QM.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Cryo-Electron Microscopy Reconstructions via the Log-Likelihood Hessian
QM.summary: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a technique in structural biology which is used to produce high-resolution 3D reconstructions of molecules. One common step in the cryo-EM pipeline involves ab-initio single-particle reconstruction (SPR). This is a type of inverse-problem which takes as input a collection of 2D-images -- each a projection of a molecule from an unknown viewing-angle -- and attempts to reconstruct the 3D-volume representing the underlying molecular density. Most methods for solving SPR search for a solution which optimizes a posterior likelihood of generating the observed image-data, given the reconstructed volume. Within this framework, it is natural to study the Hessian of the log- likelihood: the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the Hessian determine how the likelihood changes with respect to perturbations in the solution, which can give insight into the sensitivity of the solution to aspects of the input, such as the orientation distribution of image viewing-angles. In this paper, we describe a simple strategy for estimating the smallest eigenvalues and eigenvectors (i.e., the 'softest modes') of the Hessian of the log-likelihood for the ab-initio single-particle reconstruction problem. This strategy involves rewriting the log-likelihood as a 3D-integral. Once we have estimated the softest modes, we can use them to determine which parts of the reconstructed volume are trustworthy, and which are unreliable, and how this unreliability might depend on the data-set and the imaging parameters. We believe that this kind of analysis can be used alongside more traditional strategies for sensitivity analysis, as well as in other applications, such as free-energy estimation.

QM.title: Bridging the Modality Bottleneck in Pathology MIL through Molecularly Guided Feature Adaptation
QM.summary: Multiple instance learning (MIL) is the dominant framework for whole-slide image analysis in computational pathology, typically combining a frozen patch encoder, a projection layer, and a slide-level aggregator. While encoders and aggregators have been extensively studied, the projection layer remains a largely morphology-only bottleneck. This limits endpoints such as biomarker status and survival, which are governed by a molecular state that is not fully captured by H&E morphology. We introduce Molecularly Informed Staining Transform (MIST), a plug-in replacement for the MIL projection layer that uses paired spatial transcriptomics only during training to construct virtual molecular stains. MIST clusters gene expression profiles into cross-modal prototypes, anchors them in the frozen foundation model feature space, and uses them to reorganize H&E patch features along molecularly guided axes. It requires no transcriptomics at inference and can be inserted before standard MIL aggregators. We evaluate MIST across 23 downstream tasks and 8 MIL aggregators. MIST improves 240 of 256 configurations over the standard projection layer, with an average gain of +3.5%, observed consistently across endpoint types: +5.2% on survival prediction, +3.3% on tissue subtyping, and +2.6% on biomarker prediction. Ablations confirm that gene-derived prototypes are the primary source of the gains, while spatial, biological, and pathological analyses show that cross-modal prototype affinities capture spatially coherent molecular programs from H&E alone.

QM.title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
QM.summary: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.
QM.comment: 31 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/ZhaokangLiang123/CellCanon

QM.title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction
QM.summary: Foundation-model predictors of perturbation response are evaluated primarily by aggregate accuracy. Using their predictions to prioritize experiments requires assessing each prediction's reliability. We audit the state-transition (ST) decoder used in STATE across three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, and Tahoe-x1) and four cell lines under CRISPRi. The decoder's first attention layer has a low-rank output. Projecting this output onto 4-32 fixed directions estimated from training activations preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC). This low-rank attention bottleneck bounds the decoder's reliability by distance to training responses: PDC declines as the cosine distance from a perturbation's observed response to its nearest training response increases. We propose predicted-NN-distance, the cosine distance from a predicted response to its nearest training response, as a per-prediction confidence score. The score has a mean absolute Spearman correlation of 0.81 with PDC, close to the 0.88 obtained with the observed response. Thresholds calibrated on this score transfer across encoders and cell lines, and the score remains predictive of PDC for drug perturbations.
QM.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Biomolecules.title: Kinetic models of a K channel with 2 stage voltage sensor activation and an opening step
Biomolecules.summary: The activation of a K channel with 2 voltage sensors and a separate opening step may be described by a 4 state kinetic equation. If $k_{o}$ and $k_{c}$ are the opening and closing rates, and $α$ and $β$ are the voltage sensor rates such that $k_{o}$ $\ggα,k_{c}\ggβ$ and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the kinetic equation may be reduced to a 3 state model where the effective backward rate from the activated-open state is $2βk_{c}/(k_{o}+k_{c})$. However, if a K channel voltage sensor activates in 2 stages, and there is a separate opening step, the occupation probabilities of the states of the channel satisfy a 10 state kinetic equation. When the time constants of the characteristic equation for each voltage sensor differ by an order of magnitude, and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the open state probability is proportional to $n^{2}$, where $n$ satisfies a rate equation, and the derived rates have a similar voltage dependence to the rates $α_{n}$ and $β_{n}$ from voltage clamp data.

Biomolecules.title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking
Biomolecules.summary: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.
Biomolecules.comment: 17 pages, 5 figures; accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 AI4DD Workshop

Biomolecules.title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
Biomolecules.summary: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.
Biomolecules.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 23 pages, 10 figures, including supplementary material. The first three authors contributed equally. BILBY-PRO dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/HFMI-PROFOUND/BILBY-PRO ; BILBY-MD code: https://github.com/PROFOUND-HFMI/BILBY-MD

Biomolecules.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Annealing for Protein Side-Chain Optimization: A Feasibility Study
Biomolecules.summary: Hybrid quantum-classical annealing solvers are moving from research laboratories toward industrial use, but their advantage over classical optimization appears to be confined to a narrow class of problems. A recent systematic benchmark of the D-Wave hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers, across several classes of optimization problems, found it to be most competitive on binary quadratic programs, while noting that few industrial problems take this form. Therefore, identifying real-world industrial problems that can be modeled with this structure is a key challenge. We propose protein side-chain optimization, a core step of computational protein design, as one of these problems: it is natively a binary quadratic program, and its application context requires pools of low-energy solutions, which annealers naturally return. In this feasibility study, we test whether the competitiveness of the hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers extends to this problem. On 40 instances derived from 20 experimentally determined protein structures with up to about 200 amino acids and 2000 binary variables, we compare the results achieved with a hybrid solver, run for 5 seconds, against those of the commercial solver Gurobi, run for 10 seconds, 1000 seconds, and 4 hours. The hybrid solver reaches the certified optimum whenever one is available, matches Gurobi's performance on smaller instances, and outperforms it on larger instances, finding lower-energy solutions. These results show that the competitiveness of the hybrid solver on binary quadratic programs, so far observed only on a synthetic benchmark, extends to a real-world problem. This motivates comparisons with classical heuristics specific to protein side-chain optimization.

QM.title: Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
QM.summary: Models of collective motion usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces, despite empirical evidence for many-body effects. We introduce the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), which adapts the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) of interatomic potentials to self-propelled agents. dACE provides a systematically improvable, exactly equivariant expansion of an agent's acceleration that splits uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions, along with a self term for the agent's own past motion that is fitted so that it does not absorb the interactions. On simulated collectives in two and three dimensions with known rules, dACE recovers the interaction law body order by body order from little data, while the neural model SocialNet, the current closest competitor, needs more data, has much larger errors on many-body or chiral rules and is restricted to 2D. On real data sets of tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, the laws learned by dACE agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's. The learned laws are interpretable, and in the shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. Finally, we show that next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than the interactions, and suggest more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.
QM.comment: 19 pages, 10 figures

QM.title: Pattern selection and biomass shifts in a vegetation model with nonlocal competition and Allee activation
QM.summary: We study a single-species vegetation model in which a strong Allee effect acts locally and competition acts through a nonlocal kernel, and we describe the kernel with the one-parameter family of q-Gaussians, which goes from compact support to power-law tails. The local activation introduced by the Allee effect allows a finite-wavelength instability even when the Fourier transform of the kernel is positive, so Gaussian and heavy-tailed kernels can produce patterns. We derive in closed form the coefficients of the hexagonal amplitude equations and verify them against independent numerical steady states. The quadratic coefficient $Q$ results from the balance between the curvature of the local growth and the competitive inhibition at the pattern scale, and at onset its sign depends only on the fraction of the local activation that diffusion removes at the critical wavenumber. The same coefficient controls the morphology, since spots, labyrinths and gaps appear with pairwise competition only as $Q$ changes sign, and the amplitude equations predict the choice between hexagons and stripes in every simulated state in which the cubic truncation holds. It also controls the total biomass, which increases for spots and decreases for gaps.

QM.title: scDNM-VAE enables directly inspectable deep clustering of single-cell RNA-seq data through signed dendritic gating
QM.summary:
Deep clustering models for single-cell RNA sequencing often assign cells through latent or centroid-based mechanisms that are difficult to inspect. We introduce scDNM-VAE (single-cell Dendritic Neuron Model Variational Autoencoder), a deep clustering framework that combines a variational autoencoder with a dendritic neuron-inspired head. Cluster assignments are governed by learnable signed synaptic weights and thresholds: the weight sign determines the direction of a gate's response to a latent coordinate, its magnitude controls steepness, and the weight-threshold pair determines the transition location. The trained clustering function can therefore be inspected directly without fitting a post-hoc explanation model.
  We benchmark scDNM-VAE on four datasets spanning immune, cortical, cardiac, and hematopoietic cells against scVI followed by KMeans and an MLP-DEC ablation. scDNM-VAE performs better than scVI on PBMC3k, comparably on the Human Heart Cell Atlas and Paul15, and worse on Zeisel, while producing biologically coherent marker-gene signatures. Ablating each cluster's three highest-magnitude synaptic dimensions causes numerically greater reassignment than random-dimension ablation across all datasets, but the margins are modest and negligible on Zeisel. These results show that signed dendritic gating supports competitive clustering with a parameter-inspectable decision function, while indicating that decision-relevant information is distributed across the latent space.
QM.comment: 39 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Supplementary information available from the authors

QM.title: Leveraging deep generative modelling at the agent level in discrete-event simulations
QM.summary: Emulators are often invoked to facilitate parameter inference in computationally intensive agent-based simulations (ABSs). Most approaches, however, require a large sample of pre-existing outputs on which such emulators can be trained. For computationally intensive simulations, this sample can be prohibitively expensive to generate. We propose a new approach to leverage emulators at the agent level in event-based ABSs to reduce the computational requirements of the simulation itself. We demonstrate this in a computationally intensive ``multi-disease'' ABS, Thanzi La Onse, which self-consistently simulates a wide range of medical conditions in a population. By applying conditional tabular generative adversarial networks to replace the modelling of one of the simulated causes of ill health, road traffic injuries (RTIs), we are able to improve its simulation run-time by 86.6% (95% bootstrap confidence interval [85.2, 88.1]), while recovering the evolution of cause-specific mean disability adjusted life years with a 13% error, despite the low assumed incidence of fatal RTIs (~2%). Crucially, we do so while retaining the full ABS framework, and correctly recovering multi-disease dynamics. This represents a crucial step towards enabling full-model emulators for very computationally intensive simulations, and making large ABS amenable to rigorous parameter inference and a full understanding of parameter sensitivity.
QM.comment: Accepted for publication by the Journal of The Royal Society Interface

QM.title: scTREAT: Latent Diffusion for Single-Cell Drug-Response Prediction
QM.summary: Generating drug-induced transcriptional responses requires a model to account for cellular background together with molecular identity and dose. We present scTREAT, the first diffusion framework to factorize state and drug guidance for single-cell drug-response prediction. A shared latent expression space connects baseline and response, while Guided Decomposable Attention (GD-Attn) injects a baseline representation and a dose-conditioned molecular embedding. Independent channel dropout exposes four conditioning states during training; inference combines three conditional predictions with separately specified state and drug coefficients, and dose modulates drug-guidance strength. On condition-level pseudobulk profiles derived from the Tahoe-100M single-cell atlas, scTREAT achieves the best value on 10 of 12 metrics for unseen cell line-drug combinations (UC) and 11 of 12 for unseen drugs (UD). Ablations examine condition injection, molecular representation, and guidance design. On UD, the relative gains over the second-best model reach 36.11% and 34.21% for DEG logFC-Spearman and logFC-Pearson. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining shared latent expression modeling with explicit state and drug conditioning for response prediction.
QM.comment: 16 pages

QM.title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
QM.summary: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

QM.title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
QM.summary: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.
QM.comment: Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026, Findings Track. 10 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables

QM.title: Personalized health coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories
QM.summary: Personalized health coaching requires moving beyond retrospective wearable summaries toward quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions. We introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age metric built from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively captured by consumer wearables. Across the WEAR-ME (N=2,780), All of Us (N=22,748), and longitudinal Fitbit (N=1,464) cohorts, CHA aligns with established cardiometabolic health constructs and improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index. To enable prospective behavioral optimization, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned wearable world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of longitudinal sensor data from approximately 100,000 participants. SensorWM accurately forecasts multi-week physiological responses to candidate lifestyle changes ($R^2=0.664$), outperforming generic time-series foundation models while preserving downstream clinical signal for diabetes, hypertension, and other health outcomes. Finally, we integrate CHA and SensorWM into an agentic counterfactual coaching system to synthesize personalized 12-week coaching plans. In blinded paired reviews, certified lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans grounded in wearable history alone for overall quality (71.4%, P < 0.001) and anticipated adherence (71.0%, P < 0.001), and board-certified clinicians judged 99.2% of counterfactual-grounded plans to meet clinical safety criteria (vs. 97.6% of comparison plans). Automated evaluations across the full cohort (N=2,780) also favored counterfactual-grounded plans. By closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction, and counterfactual coaching, our framework provides a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health.

QM.title: From Shape to Species: The Use of Persistent Homology in Restructuring the Taxonomy of \textit{Acropora} corals
QM.summary: Traditional coral taxonomy is increasingly challenged by recent advances in molecular evidence. Quantitative methods previously used to identify morphological descriptors have not been successful at detecting significant differences at the macroscale. It is of great interest to optimise methods for effectively delimiting species within the complex genus \textit{Acropora} to ensure sustainable, long-term management of these vital ecosystems. Topological Data Analysis (TDA) is designed to study the shape of data and can detect features that familiar methods overlook. This novel approach makes TDA and persistent homology a logical choice for studying coral morphology in a taxonomic context. The results show that valid topological information can be extracted from in-situ coral images and that there is great potential in further refining this method. This study is a first exploration into the potential of persistent homology in supporting the delimitation of the reef-building scleractinian corals \textit{Acropora}.

Biomolecules.title: Atomic Trajectory Modeling with State Space Models for Biomolecular Dynamics
Biomolecules.summary: Understanding the dynamic behavior of biomolecules is fundamental to elucidating biological function and facilitating drug discovery.While Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations provide a rigorous physical basis for studying these dynamics, they remain computationally expensive for long timescales.Recent deep generative models accelerate conformation generation but often either discard temporal correlations entirely or struggle to condition on the extended history required for faithful kinetics, a consequence of the effectively non-Markovian nature of partially observed subsystem coordinates.To bridge this gap, we introduce ATMOS, a novel generative framework based on State Space Models (SSM) designed to generate atom-level MD trajectories for biomolecular systems.ATMOS integrates a Pairformer-based state transition mechanism to capture temporal dependencies, with a diffusion-based module to decode trajectory frames autoregressively.We demonstrate that ATMOS achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating conformation trajectories for both protein monomers and protein-ligand systems.This work provides a unified and computationally efficient framework for biomolecular trajectory generation, taking a step toward dynamics foundation models.

Biomolecules.title: Monroe: A Molecular Foundation Model for In-Context Probabilistic Inference
Biomolecules.summary: Bioassay activity prediction is often data-limited because drug-discovery datasets rely on time-consuming and expensive wet-lab experiments for data generation and evaluation. This challenge has inspired recent research into molecular foundation models (MFMs), which aim to encode general-purpose chemical knowledge into molecular representations that generalize well in data-constrained scenarios. This paper presents Monroe, a new MFM with several innovations over the existing state of the art: increased scale allowing pre-training on over 81 million molecules from the PM6 quantum chemistry dataset; improved graph representation of stereochemistry; improved training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation; improved multi-task learning; and the use of a prior-data-fitted model (TabPFNv3) for downstream in-context prediction. Our evaluations use a principled pairwise comparison framework that measures statistically significant performance differences. Across established Polaris benchmarks, Monroe matches or exceeds existing MFMs, while on activity cliff benchmarks, designed to assess utility for molecular discovery, it achieves significant improvements over prior methods. Finally, ablation and transfer experiments show that PFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models, MiniMol and CheMeleon, yielding new state-of-the-art variants we call MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN, suggesting that our downstream adaptation strategy generalizes beyond Monroe. Source code is at github.com/blazejba/Monroe
Biomolecules.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Biomolecules.title: Protein B-factor modeling with local magnitude
Biomolecules.summary: Topological magnitude characterizes the effective size and spatial organization of metric spaces, offering a geometric approach with potential applications in molecular biology and materials science. Previous work has demonstrated its utility in modeling protein flexibility from structure, but global magnitude weighting requires dense linear systems whose computational cost increases with protein size. We introduce a local magnitude representation that retains residue-level structural information through nearest-neighbor environments. The construction is well posed and geometrically invariant, with central weighting distinguished from scalar neighborhood magnitude. Across 364 proteins, the mean within-protein fitting Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) increases from 0.725 for global magnitude to 0.728 for local magnitude. Blind-prediction experiments on 345 proteins combine each representation with identical auxiliary descriptors and evaluate random forests and gradient boosting under three validation protocols. Local features improve the primary PCC in all six model--protocol comparisons, with a maximum absolute increase of 0.008 in protein-level ten-fold gradient boosting. For a fixed feature bank, local factorization costs $O(Nk^3)$ compared with $O(N^3)$ for global factorization, where $N$ is the number of C$_α$ atoms and $k$ the neighborhood size. Timing measurements show a computational advantage of local magnitude on large structures. Within the tested single-seed configuration and distinct global and local scale banks, these results support local magnitude as a compact representation that preserves useful B-factor information while reducing feature-extraction costs for large proteins.

Biomolecules.title: BioBlobs: Unsupervised Discovery of Functional Substructures
Biomolecules.summary: Protein function is often localized to cohesive substructures, such as catalytic triads, binding pockets, and structural motifs, that occupy only a small fraction of a protein's residues. Yet existing predictive pipelines typically aggregate residue-level embeddings and do not explicitly model or infer these functional substructures, leaving the central biological question unanswered: which substructure of a protein is responsible for its function? We introduce BioBlobs, an encoder-agnostic, end-to-end differentiable framework that compresses a protein into a small set of cohesive substructures (blobs) and predicts function from these blobs alone, so that each blob corresponds to a candidate functional region. Across diverse protein function prediction tasks and both sequence-only and structure-aware protein language models, BioBlobs is competitive with strong baselines while operating on only a small fraction of residues. Trained only on protein function labels, BioBlobs recovers expert-curated functional sites in InterPro and experimentally annotated catalytic sites in the Mechanism and Catalytic Site Atlas, demonstrating unsupervised functional substructure discovery and opening a path to large-scale functional site discovery in unannotated proteins. The discovered blobs adapt their spatial scale to the task, ranging from local catalytic sites to entire structural domains. Code is available at https://github.com/OliverLaboratory/BioBlobs.
Biomolecules.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). 25 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code: https://github.com/OliverLaboratory/BioBlobs

QM.title: Health-System-Wide Mapping of Demographic Information in Routine Clinical Histopathology
QM.summary: The extent to which demographic-associated information is detectable across organs and disease states in routine clinical histopathology remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 1.3 million hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images from 257,322 patients across 25 organs, using pathology foundation-model representations and multiple-instance learning to systematically map information associated with sex, age group, and self-reported race. Across 69 organ-demographic combinations, demographic attributes were broadly recoverable, with pan-organ mean AUROCs of 0.828 for sex, 0.733 for age group, and 0.662 for self-reported race, and substantial variation across organs. Demographic-class balancing produced relatively small changes in performance, while evaluation within diagnosis-text clusters showed modest attenuation. Under training with diagnosis-based grouping, demographic-associated signals remained detectable across multiple organs, including sex in gastric tissue (AUROC 0.865), age group in breast (0.816), and self-reported race in skin (0.728). Literature-guided analysis of these settings generated candidate histomorphological and contextual explanations for further investigation. Together, these findings provide a systematic map of demographic-associated information in routine histopathology, informing investigations of its sources, assessments of potential shortcut learning, and the development of more interpretable computational pathology models.
QM.comment: 35 pages, 4 main figures, 2 supplementary figures, and 10 supplementary tables. Interactive Results Atlas and Hypothesis Explorer accompany the manuscript

QM.title: The effect of limb kinematics on the speed of a legged robot on granular media
QM.summary: Achieving effective locomotion on diverse terrestrial substrates can require subtle changes of limb kinematics. Biologically inspired legged robots (physical models of organisms) have shown impressive mobility on hard ground but suffer performance loss on unconsolidated granular materials like sand. Because comprehensive limb-ground interaction models are lacking, optimal gaits on complex yielding terrain have been determined empirically. To develop predictive models for legged devices and to provide hypotheses for biological locomotors, we systematically study the performance of SandBot, a small legged robot, on granular media as a function of gait parameters. High performance occurs only in a small region of parameter space. A previously introduced kinematic model of the robot combined with a new anisotropic granular penetration force law predicts the speed. Performance on granular media is maximized when gait parameters minimize body acceleration and limb interference, and utilize solidification features of granular media.

QM.summary: Bioassay activity prediction is often data-limited because drug-discovery datasets rely on time-consuming and expensive wet-lab experiments for data generation and evaluation. This challenge has inspired recent research into molecular foundation models (MFMs), which aim to encode general-purpose chemical knowledge into molecular representations that generalize well in data-constrained scenarios. This paper presents Monroe, a new MFM with several innovations over the existing state of the art: increased scale allowing pre-training on over 81 million molecules from the PM6 quantum chemistry dataset; improved graph representation of stereochemistry; improved training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation; improved multi-task learning; and the use of a prior-data-fitted model (TabPFNv3) for downstream in-context prediction. Our evaluations use a principled pairwise comparison framework that measures statistically significant performance differences. Across established Polaris benchmarks, Monroe matches or exceeds existing MFMs, while on activity cliff benchmarks, designed to assess utility for molecular discovery, it achieves significant improvements over prior methods. Finally, ablation and transfer experiments show that PFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models, MiniMol and CheMeleon, yielding new state-of-the-art variants we call MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN, suggesting that our downstream adaptation strategy generalizes beyond Monroe. QM.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
QM.summary: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite this broad potential impact, selection bias is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct it, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle and assumptions, and we compare methods addressing the same form of selection by their assumptions, data requirements and limitations. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R, prepares input for the external SPREG software, and provides worked examples on simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection, one of which we present in full. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with recommendations for bias-aware study design, sensitivity analysis and reporting.
QM.comment: 44 pages, 3 figures

QM.title: KineCouple: Substrate-conditioned residual readout for enzyme kinetic prediction
QM.summary: Accurate prediction of enzyme kinetic parameters can support enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling by complementing experimental characterization. Existing prediction methods often pool residue-level protein features before combining them with substrate features. Such substrate-independent pooling cannot adapt residue weighting to the substrate during aggregation, potentially diluting information relevant to a specific enzyme-substrate pair. Since the contributions of individual residues to catalysis can depend on the substrate, substrate-conditioned aggregation offers a way to emphasize residue features relevant to the prediction. We introduce KineCouple, which uses substrate queries and residue-level keys and values in cross-attention, allowing the substrate to guide residue selection before aggregation. The model preserves the global protein representation and adds a gated correction defined as the difference between the conditioned readout and a uniform readout. ProtT5 and MolT5 remain frozen, and separate models predict kcat and Km on a logarithmic scale. In pooled out-of-fold predictions on the CataPro benchmarks, KineCouple reduces kcat RMSE from 1.333 to 1.330 and increases PCC from 0.492 to 0.496 relative to reproduced CataPro. For Km, RMSE decreases from 0.998 to 0.997 and PCC increases from 0.633 to 0.634. Spearman correlation also improves for both tasks.

QM.title: ImmSET: Sequence-Based Predictor of TCR-pMHC Specificity at Scale
QM.summary: T cells are a critical component of the adaptive immune system, playing a role in infectious disease, autoimmunity, and cancer. T cell function is mediated by the T cell receptor (TCR) protein, a highly diverse receptor targeting specific peptides presented by the major histocompatibility complex (pMHCs). Predicting the specificity of TCRs for their cognate pMHCs is central to understanding adaptive immunity and enabling personalized therapies. However, accurate prediction of this protein-protein interaction remains challenging due to the extreme diversity of both TCRs and pMHCs. Here, we present ImmSET (Immune Synapse Encoding Transformer), a novel sequence-based architecture designed to model interactions among sets of variable-length biological sequences. We train this model across a range of dataset sizes and compositions and study the resulting models' generalization to pMHC targets. We describe a failure mode in prior sequence-based approaches that inflates previously reported performance on this task and show that ImmSET remains robust under stricter evaluation. In systematically testing the scaling behavior of ImmSET with training data, we show that performance scales consistently with data volume across multiple data types and compares favorably with the pre-trained protein language model ESM2 fine-tuned on the same datasets. Finally, we demonstrate that ImmSET can outperform AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3-based pipelines on TCR-pMHC specificity prediction when provided sufficient training data. This work establishes ImmSET as a scalable modeling paradigm for multi-sequence interaction problems, demonstrated in the TCR-pMHC setting but generalizable to other biological domains where high-throughput sequence-driven reasoning complements structure prediction and experimental mapping.
QM.comment: arXiv admin note: This submission has been withdrawn because it does not meet arXiv's research content quality standards

QM.title: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks
QM.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.

Biomolecules.title: Co-folding model guided by structural proteomics
Biomolecules.summary: Proximity-inducing drugs, including PROTACs, represent a promising therapeutic modality. Their activity is driven by the geometry of the assembled ternary complex, which determines whether the target is ubiquitinated. Co-folding models perform poorly in these cases due to scarcity of training data and the dynamic nature of such complexes. Structural proteomics can supply the missing geometric information and steer the model towards an accurate prediction. However, current models accept only positive signals, while a differential structural mass-spectrometry experiment also reports negative signals. We introduce AIMS-Fold, an inference-time guidance layer built on Boltz-2 that requires no retraining and accepts repulsive constraints alongside attractive ones. We tested AIMS-Fold on 28 PROTAC, glue and antibody complexes that Boltz-2 fails to predict. From only five generated models, guidance recovers the correct conformation in 64% of cases. The gap does not close with scale: across 100 models and 20 seeds, unguided Boltz-2 reaches 14% while AIMS-Fold reaches 86%. Repulsive constraints alone recover the correct conformation on some systems, occasionally exceeding the matched attractive constraints. Taken together, these results demonstrate the strength of utilizing the full structural proteomics signal, positive and negative, to steer generative models toward the correct conformation, addressing a central problem in rational degrader design.

Biomolecules.title: HyPLM Technical Report
Biomolecules.summary: Protein language models (PLMs) are standard tools for variant-effect prediction, protein annotation and design, but the compute needed to train and serve them keeps growing. We present HyPLM-Flash, an efficient and open PLM trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team. HyPLM-Flash is a 650-million-parameter masked language model trained on 726 billion tokens, 0.73 times the data of ESM-2 650M and a fifth to an eighth of the data of E1-600M and ESM C 600M. It runs on an inference engine with fused kernels and INT8 matrix multiplication, embedding about 130,000 residues per second on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, 1.9 to 2.7 times faster than other 600M-class encoders. In a matched evaluation against 28 public checkpoints on 32 tasks, HyPLM-Flash reaches a ProteinGym zero-shot Spearman correlation of 0.409, statistically tied with ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M, and the highest organismal-fitness score among self-supervised single-sequence models. It gives the best long-range contact precision of all models evaluated, including ESM-2 15B and ESM C 6B, and a lower masked-residue loss than ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M on held-out sequences and on recently released PDB chains. Matching state-of-the-art accuracy at a fraction of the training and inference cost, HyPLM-Flash sets a new Pareto frontier for protein language models. We have released the model weights and the inference engine at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/hyra-results/tree/main.

Biomolecules.title: HyInv Technical Report
Biomolecules.summary: Inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences for a given protein backbone, and screening needs many candidates that are both diverse and well folded. We present HyInv, a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team: pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning. At inference, a grouped draft-and-rewrite sampler that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures improves refolding TM-score at matched diversity. An optimized implementation with BF16 numerics designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and an exact FP32 path that returns the reference sequences is 8.7 times faster. Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2. The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept, and loop redesign. We have released our code and model at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results/tree/main/AI4Science/hyinv.

Biomolecules.title: OriDynamics: Towards a World Model for Biomolecular Dynamics
Biomolecules.summary: Biomolecular recognition and regulation depend on atomic interactions that change as molecular partners fluctuate and adopt alternative conformations. Modeling these processes requires ensembles that capture both conformational diversity and coordinated atomic fluctuations between interacting molecules. Here we present OriDynamics, a unified framework for all-atom ensemble generation across protein monomers and complexes with small molecules or protein partners. OriDynamics introduces a latent ensemble decomposition that couples broad conformational exploration in a compact structural latent space with local all-atom sampling around generated proposals. Ensemble-level supervision constrains mean positions, fluctuation amplitudes and joint coordinate covariance to capture coordinated atomic variability within and between molecular partners. Across benchmarks of proteins and their complexes, OriDynamics demonstrates superior overall performance in conformational coverage, atomic fluctuation fidelity and interaction geometry compared with leading baselines. Application studies further demonstrate recovery of alternative functional conformations and partner-dependent changes in conformational ensembles alongside sampling of configurations associated with ligand dissociation. These capabilities provide a foundation for a biomolecular world model that represents accessible molecular states and their dependence on interaction context.
Biomolecules.comment: 29 pages, 6 main figures and 5 supplementary figures. Includes supplementary information

Biomolecules.title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
Biomolecules.summary: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.

QM.title: AI-based characterization of lymphoid structures and the tumor microenvironment reveals lower mature tertiary lymphoid structures, lymph-node follicles, and plasma cells after neoadjuvant therapy in lung squamous cell carcinoma
QM.summary: Mature, germinal centre-bearing tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) and mature lymph node follicles (secondary lymphoid structures, SLS) sustain the plasma cell response that shapes outcome and immunotherapy benefit in lung cancer. How this loco-regional axis differs between neoadjuvant-treated and therapy-naive tumors is poorly defined. We analyzed H&E whole-slide images of resected tumors and paired proximal and distal lymph nodes from matched neoadjuvant-treated (neoLUSC, n=20) and therapy-naive (naivLUSC, n=20) lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) patients. Aignostics Atlas H&E Tissue Analysis (HETA) models quantified cell densities per tissue compartment and cell-cell co-localization; a dedicated deep-learning model validated against pathologist annotations detected TLS and SLS and graded their maturity. Prognostic value was tested in an independent cohort (n=458; 46 treated). In neoLUSC tumors, stromal plasma cell density was 72% (p=0.004) and stromal lymphocyte density 48% (p=0.015) lower than in naivLUSC; macrophages and granulocytes did not differ significantly. Total and immature TLS did not differ, whereas mature TLS in the tumor (p=0.034) and mature SLS in the tumor-distal lymph node (p=0.003) were lower in neoLUSC patients. Peri-TLS plasma cell density correlated with tumor lymphocyte density in naivLUSC (rho=0.54, p=0.017) but not in neoLUSC tumors (rho=0.07). In the validation cohort, stromal plasma cell density (HR 0.69, p=0.011) and lymphocyte-plasma cell co-localization (HR 0.66, p=0.004) were associated with longer survival, and neoadjuvant status with shorter survival (HR 1.50, p=0.026). Neoadjuvant therapy is thus associated with fewer mature lymphoid structures and weaker coupling of the humoral compartment to the tumor rather than uniformly lower immune readouts. The stromal plasma cell/co-localization axis is a candidate prognostic biomarker.

QM.title: Toward Controlling Biology with Language: Offline Learning of Prompt-Conditioned Interventions for Cells, Organoids, and Biobots
QM.summary: Natural language has become an interface to code, images and molecules, but not to living matter: a stimulus applied to cells has no fixed linguistic meaning, and every paired example of an instruction and its outcome costs a wet-lab experiment. We ask how far an existing archive of experiments can take this interface, using xenobots, motile multicellular constructs made of frog cells, stimulated by a single electrical pulse of varying duration. We re-track 155 archived recordings with two independent methods, measure what the pulse does from each bot's own behaviour before and after it, and separate behaviours the pulse controls from behaviours it does not. Longer pulses stop bots and short pulses leave them moving, sometimes faster; turning direction and starting from rest do not depend on duration, and restarting at most weakly. We then replace hand-made behaviour labels with a blind language critic: fresh sessions of a multimodal language model read plots of each bot and score how well its behaviour matches each of 176 instructions. The critic agrees with the measured labels whenever its plots contain the information the labels are defined on, and dose curves learned from its scores match those learned from the measurements. A prompt-to-intervention model trained only on critic scores maps unseen instructions, including negations, to the right end of the dose range on unseen bots, as well as the same model trained on measured labels. The archive therefore supports a calibrated, refusing language interface for the three behaviours a pulse can set, and identifies, rather than hides, the behaviours it cannot.

Archive re-tracked with two independent trackers; measured outcomes for eight behaviours; blind language critic validated against measurements; prompt-to-intervention model outputs a dose-response curve and is evaluated on unseen instructions and unseen bots

QM.title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
QM.summary: The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.

QM.title: Trajectory Inference of Human Aging from Cross-Sectional DNA Methylation Data
QM.summary: DNA methylation (DNAm) serves as one of the most robust molecular biomarkers of biological aging. While conventional epigenetic clocks accurately predict chronological age from high-dimensional CpG profiles, they treat aging as a static regression task, meaning they can only output a single score rather than simulating how an entire profile continuously changes over time. To reconstruct these continuous dynamics, we frame lifelong human epigenetic aging as a trajectory inference problem across discrete age snapshots derived from widely available cross-sectional data. We introduce a two-stage computational pipeline: first, an age-regularized Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maps high-dimensional CpG profiles onto a chronologically ordered latent manifold while preserving a generative decoder bridge back to the original methylation space. Second, we model the continuous movement across this latent space via Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT) that unifies deterministic drift, random diffusion, and non-conservative mass changes. By resolving this RUOT formulation using the DeepRUOT framework, our model fluidly accommodates population-level density shifts like survivorship bias and cellular attrition without requiring rigid biological priors. Evaluated on a large-scale, 80-year pan-tissue dataset, our model demonstrates robust distribution interpolation and uncovers a prominent late-life surge in the learned growth field that mathematically captures the variance expansion driven by stochastic epigenetic drift. Finally, by decoding continuous latent paths back to individual CpG sites, we reconstruct and empirically verify distinct biological aging archetypes, offering a rigorous, generative paradigm for simulating human molecular aging.

QM.title: Surf_2_Volume: A Python Toolbox for Cortical Ribbon Based CIFTI to NIfTI Conversion
QM.summary: Many neuroimaging workflows require NIfTI label volumes, whereas cortical parcellations are increasingly distributed in CIFTI surface space. Existing conversion tools offer several mapping settings. In nearest vertex mapping, a small distance can leave cortical voxels unlabeled, whereas a larger distance can extend labels beyond the intended cortical region. Choosing among settings is difficult when no paired volume atlas is available. We present Surf_2_Volume, a Python toolbox that projects discrete cortical labels within an adjustable cortical ribbon. Users can specify the ribbon threshold directly or use an optional procedure that ranks candidate thresholds using information from the source atlas. This procedure ranks 12 thresholds by differences between each label's proportion of source cortical vertices and its proportion of output voxels, without using a published volume atlas for selection. We evaluated four configurations from two atlas families: Yeo2011 parcellations with 7 and 17 networks, represented by 51 and 114 spatial components, and Schaefer2018 100-parcel atlases with 7 and 17 network assignments. All four selected sets included threshold 0.05, which had the highest macro-Dice and macro-Jaccard among the tested package thresholds. Eleven of the 12 selected outputs had higher macro-Dice than the best tested Connectome Workbench mapping for their atlas. In 24 HCP participants, all 12 selected outputs had higher participant-level mean parcel time-series concordance than every tested Workbench mapping (all within-atlas FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Surf_2_Volume provides a reproducible way to generate and select volume atlas candidates when only a surface parcellation is available, while retaining alternatives for different coverage and signal-extraction needs.

QM.title: stMIND: Learning multiscale interaction dynamics from spatial-temporal transcriptomics
QM.summary: Interactions within local cellular neighborhoods and across broader tissue scales jointly govern molecular state transitions and morphogenesis during development and regeneration. While time-resolved spatial transcriptomics simultaneously profiles gene expression and spatial coordinates, destructive sequencing samples distinct cells at each time point, leaving intermediate trajectories and multiscale intercellular interactions unobserved. Building upon our interacting mean-field neural stochastic differential equation framework, we present stMIND (Spatiotemporal Multiscale Interaction Neural Dynamics), a continuous-time generative framework that infers coupled molecular, spatial, and proliferation dynamics from unmatched spatiotemporal snapshots. stMIND decomposes cellular expression velocity vector/drift into three interpretable operators: a cell-intrinsic program, a local graph-difference attention operator that aggregates relative expression differences and spatial geometry within a co-evolving physical radius, and a nonlocal mean-field attention operator that captures long-range population context beyond the immediate neighborhood. By evolving dynamic spatial neighborhoods alongside cellular migration and enforcing orthogonality between intrinsic and interaction-driven drifts, stMIND resolves scale-specific intercellular influences through optimal transport in joint expression-position space. In axolotl and zebrafish benchmarks, stMIND leads in expression prediction, anatomical consistency and spatial coherence. Ablations confirm the need to combine disjoint local and nonlocal operators. It reveals a regenerative transition in axolotl telencephalon 10 to 15 days after injury, with a drift energy surge followed by nonlocal dominance and local counterbalance varying by cell type in reactive ependymoglial niches. It tracks developmental vector fields across zebrafish stages.

QM.title: BioMARS 2.0: a robotic biologist for formulating and adapting biological experiments
QM.summary: Biological experimentation is not reducible to a single optimization problem, but requires decisions at multiple levels of abstraction: translating scientific knowledge into experimental procedures, adapting culture conditions to measured phenotypes and selecting interventions that test biological hypotheses. Automating experimental execution does not, by itself, determine which experiments should be performed next or how they should change in response to biological feedback. Here we introduce BioMARS, a human-in-the-loop multi-agent robotic system that connects knowledge-guided experimental decision-making with robotic execution and biological feedback. At the procedural level, BioMARS generated literature-grounded protocols and traceable action plans, improving expert-reviewed protocol quality scores across four model backends. At the parametric level, BioMARS used image-derived phenotypes from robotic retinal organoid culture to select subsequent experimental conditions, with higher reported scores in later rounds of the three-round experiment. At the intervention level, BioMARS nominated drug-repurposing candidates from biomedical evidence and advanced six candidates to wet-lab testing by researchers. Together, these studies demonstrate feedback-driven robotic biological experimentation within a framework that supports decisions about experimental procedures, culture conditions and biological interventions.

QM.title: Conservative Continuous-Time Treatment Optimization
QM.summary: Finding optimal treatment plans in continuous time is crucial for personalized medicine. Existing methods, however, do not explicitly optimize treatment plans and instead focus solely on predicting treatment effects. Naive optimization over these treatment-response models can exploit model errors, resulting in plans that appear optimal under the learned model but perform poorly in practice. To mitigate model exploitation, we propose SigCTO (Signature-based Conservative Treatment Optimization), a conservative framework for continuous-time treatment optimization. We derive a path-space regularizer based on signature-kernel maximum mean discrepancy that penalizes treatment plans for which predicted and true responses differ. Under suitable assumptions, the regularizer allows for consistent estimation, and the regularized objective upper bounds the true treatment cost. Experiments on pharmacometric simulators show that SigCTO finds treatment plans with lower ground-truth costs than state-of-the-art baselines. On real-world ICU data, SigCTO predicts treatment cost more accurately than baselines, and the regularizer detects prediction errors.
QM.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

QM.title: Better Protein Function Prediction by Modeling Survivorship Bias
QM.summary: Predicting whether a protein sequence possesses a biochemical property of interest is important for understanding and designing protein functionality. Modern protein sequence databases provide valuable training data for functional prediction, but they exhibit survivorship bias: natural selection favors variants that support organismal survival while eliminating many others before they can be observed, complicating classifier training. This setting motivates positive-unlabeled (PU) learning, which treats observed functional sequences as positive and unobserved sequences as unlabeled rather than nonfunctional. However, existing protein PU methods do not account for cross-sequence heterogeneity in evolutionary accessibility: sequences one nucleotide mutation away from a common variant arise far more readily than distant ones. We introduce PULSE: PU Learning with Surveillance and Evolution, a framework that trains a probabilistic classifier for a target protein function using an evolution-aware observation likelihood. When considering functionality of proteins with high genomic sequence coverage, PULSE combines a probabilistic classifier that estimates whether an amino acid sequence performs the target function with an evolutionary model that estimates the likelihood that its encoding nucleotide sequences emerge and are detected based on mutational accessibility, parental prevalence, and surveillance e!ciency. By coupling these two components, PULSE treats the absence of an evolutionarily accessible sequence as stronger evidence of non-functionality than the absence of one unlikely to arise. Tested on eleven tasks focusing on multiple Spike protein properties spanning five SARS-CoV-2 variants, PULSE ranks first or second on all of them, and achieves the best overall performance among all methods, including standard PU learning, one-class classification methods, and protein language models.
QM.comment: 21 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables

QM.title: Reproducible quantum clustering for single-cell transcriptome atlases
QM.summary: Current single-cell clustering pipelines discard most genes and can yield inconsistent clusters across random seeds. We introduce KQE-2, a training-free hybrid quantum-classical framework for reproducible whole-transcriptome clustering. KQE-2 maps cells into entanglement-free quantum states, enabling exact feature evaluation on classical hardware and direct checks on a quantum processor. Theoretically, we prove that removing entanglement is necessary and sufficient to bound single-qubit feature variance locally. Practically, while retraining scVI shifted 14% of cells and altered rare-type markers and drug targets, KQE-2 delivered identical biology across runs. On standard highly variable genes, the quantum encoding alone raised accuracy on a developing cortex from 0.61 to 0.79. KQE-2 scales to 11.4 million nuclei on one server, outperforming the compared methods on eight of ten complete atlases (and within the best method's run-to-run range on two), and leads on six even under standard downstream clustering.
QM.comment: 28 pages; 5 figures and 1 table in the main text; 5 Extended Data figures, 5 Extended Data tables; Supplementary Information with 2 figures and 15 tables

QM.title: Pulsatile Endocrine Regulation with a Releasable Hormone Pool: Impulsive Feedback Model
QM.summary: An impulsive model of endocrine regulation equipped with frequency- and amplitude-modulated pulsatile feedback is extended to study the dynamical effects pertaining to limitations due to the releasable hormone pool. The model describes a three-hormone regulatory loop and is applicable to endocrine systems such as the reproductive, stress, and growth hormone axes. Conditions guaranteeing the existence and uniqueness of a periodic solution with a single feedback-triggered impulse per period (a 1-cycle) are derived, together with monotonicity properties of its characteristics. An explicit Jacobian formula is obtained to assess local orbital stability. Model analysis demonstrates that a reduced hormone-pool replenishment rate produces a lower-amplitude, higher-frequency 1-cycle. This behavior is consistent with experimentally observed alterations in testosterone regulation in aging human males.

QM.title: EvoSurv: Evolution-Aware Multimodal Survival Modeling Reveals Complementary Prognostic Signals
QM.summary: Accurate cancer survival prediction remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity. Although multimodal survival models integrate clinical and molecular data, they often overlook evolutionary information encoded in genomic alterations. To address this gap, we developed eTime, a 38-dimensional evolutionary representation comprising eight feature groups that characterize clonal and subclonal mutation burden, mutational spectra, functional consequences, copy-number alterations, and anoikis-related genomic changes. We further developed EvoSurv, a multimodal survival framework integrating eTime with clinical variables and RNA expression. Across six TCGA cancer cohorts comprising 2,782 patients, EvoSurv achieved the highest mean concordance index (C-index) in all six cancers, averaging 0.663 and outperforming three state-of-the-art survival prediction methods. More importantly, we assessed whether evolutionary features provide additional prognostic information beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors. eTime remained significantly associated with survival in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) after adjustment for clinical variables and RNA-derived risk scores. Feature-group analyses further revealed cancer-specific prognostic patterns. In HNSC, T>G substitutions were associated with increased mortality risk after clinical and molecular adjustment, including in HPV-negative patients, with supporting evidence from an independent CPTAC-HNSCC cohort. Overall, these findings demonstrate that eTime captures survival-associated evolutionary information and highlight its potential to provide prognostic value beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors.
QM.comment: 11 pages, 3 figures

Biomolecules.title: Symmetry-Induced Conservation Laws, Three-Channel Attribution, and Solid-Phase Recycling in Prebiotic Enantiomeric Excess Amplification
Biomolecules.summary: Enantiomeric excess ($\mathrm{ee}$) is the primary observable used to quantify chiral amplification across prebiotic chemistry, asymmetric autocatalysis, and multiphase crystallization. Because $\mathrm{ee} = Δ/ M$ is the ratio of net chiral excess $Δ= L - D$ to total chiral mass $M = L + D$, identical increases in $\mathrm{ee}$ can arise either by generating net chiral excess through parity-breaking reactions or by depleting total chiral mass through symmetric phase or oligomer partitioning. Here we establish a pathwise conservation law and a model-free three-channel attribution identity for $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric reaction networks. In any closed network without autocatalytic feedback or epimerization, net chiral excess is conserved along every stochastic trajectory ($Δ(t) = Δ(0)$), locking liquid-phase amplification to cumulative mass loss ($\mathrm{ee}_f = \mathrm{ee}_0 M_0 / M_f$). Re-analyzing seven experimental systems shows that standalone phase removal (Channel R) loses $91.7\%$--$98.9\%$ of chiral solute into racemic sediment in closed batches and washes out under open racemic inflow. Coupling eutectic partitioning (Channel R) with solid/solution racemization recycling (Channel B) converts the precipitated solid into homochiral product ($96.5\%$ recoverable homochiral crystal mass at $96.5\%$ total and $100.0\%$ solid $\mathrm{ee}$), whereas coupling evaporative concentration with liquid-phase autocatalysis crosses the open-flow bifurcation threshold against continuous racemic dilution ($81.9\%$ homochiral yield at $92.9\%$ active chiral $\mathrm{ee}$).
